Bernhard, Count of the Marck, or called the
Chemical Count.
He wrote a treatise in 4 parts and some epistles,
in which he shows the reader with all sincerity
and truth what he worked on and
where he achieved nothing;
On the other hand, he indicates the <term>first matter <note>original: "f. mater," likely an abbreviation for the Latin *prima materia*, the primordial base substance required to begin the alchemical transformation</note></term> along with the way quite clearly;
whoever does not wish to be wiser than what this Count
has written can find a great light:
but whoever will not believe him
and works with the materials that
he rejects seeks his own ruin.

<summary>This page introduces Bernard, Count of the Marck (better known as Bernard of Trevisan), a celebrated alchemist praised here for his honesty regarding his failed experiments. The text suggests that his writings provide a "great light" for those who follow his specific instructions on the "first matter."</summary>

Regarding this, the highly learned **LIPSIUS** <note>Justus Lipsius (1547–1606), a famous humanist scholar</note> beautifully discourses in his magnificent book, *Physiology of the Stoics* <note>Latin: "Physiologia Stoicorum"</note>, book 1, dissertation 7 and book 2, dissertation 8.

benefit of the moist nature <note>Latin: "beneficio naturæ humidæ"</note> (as **HERMES** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom the foundational texts of alchemy are attributed</note> calls it); when the air is moist and wet, this spirit is most frequently led to the earth. dwells. However, because of its subtlety and volatility, it finds no permanent residence even in the bare, rough, porous earth. It unites with this salt as if with its magnet, which **SENDIVOGIUS** <note>Michael Sendivogius (1566–1636), a famous Polish alchemist known for his theories on the "food of life" found in the air</note> calls the <term>Chalybs</term> <note>Latin: "Chalybs," meaning steel; in alchemy, this refers to a "magnetic" substance that attracts the celestial spirit</note>, *which is found in the belly of the Ram* <note>Latin: "qui invenitur in ventre arietis"</note>. For *salt is easily joined to salt, and heat to heat* <note>Latin: "Sal enim sali, calor calori facilè jungitur"</note>, as the aforementioned **SENDIVOGIUS** has philosophized at greater length.

And from the union of these two, *by the mediation of the ethereal spirit* <note>Latin: "mediante spiritu æthereo"</note>, arises the <term>radical moisture</term> <note>Latin: "Humidum radicale." In early medicine and alchemy, this was the essential fluid of life that maintained the "natural heat" of a body</note>, the foundational moisture and the natural balm of all things, *which consists of Mercury and Sulfur, as the moist and the warm, and in Salt* <note>Latin: "qui ex Mercur. & Sulphure, ceu humido & calido, constat, & in Sale..." The text cuts off here, referring to the "Tria Prima" or three primary substances of Paracelsian alchemy: Mercury, Sulfur, and Salt</note>

Regarding the other small treatises which were attached and published by the aforementioned **Dr. Tancke**, these are very good—especially the *Dialogue* <note>original: "DIALOGUS"</note>, the *Sayings of Alanus* <note>original: "DICTA ALANI"; likely referring to Alan of Lille, a 12th-century scholar to whom alchemical works were often attributed</note>, and the *Metallurgy* <note>original: "METALLURGIA"</note>. # Preface
## Of Count Bernhard to all Lovers of the True Art.

Having experienced the errors and deceptions of the alchemists and false *slanderers* <note>original: "Calumnianten"</note>, who with their frauds do nothing other than make our worthy Art and science hated and despised: I have wished, for the *remedy* <note>original: "Remedirung"</note> and prevention of such mischief, to faithfully warn all truth-loving and sincere hearts, so that they may take good care of their fortunes and escape the snares and seductions of the deceivers who misuse this noble Art. Instead, they may find the right path according to the direction and guidance of the true *Philosophers* <note>In this context, "Philosophers" refers to the historical alchemists who sought the secrets of nature.</note> experienced in the genuine Art. It is a common proverb: that one may indeed listen to everyone, but to grant belief to everyone's words, without certain *proofs* <note>original: "Probationes"</note> and evidence, would be...

### The Emerald Tablet.

*It is true, without falsehood, certain and most true: that which is below is like that which is above, and that which is above is like that which is below, to accomplish the miracles of one thing. And just as all things proceeded from one, by the meditation of one; so all things were born from this one thing, by adaptation. Its father is the Sun, its mother is the Moon. The wind carried it in its belly, its nurse is the earth. The father of all perfection <note>original Latin: "telesmi"; a term derived from the Greek "telesmos," referring to the completion or the spiritual "goal" of the alchemical work</note> of the whole world is here. Its power is complete if it is turned toward the earth. You shall separate the earth from the fire, the subtle from the gross, gently and with great ingenuity. It ascends from the earth to the heaven, and again it descends to the earth, and receives the power of the higher and the lower things. Thus you have the glory of the whole world. Therefore all darkness shall flee from you. This is the strong fortitude of all fortitude, because it will overcome every subtle thing and penetrate every solid thing. Thus the world was created. From this shall come marvelous adaptations, the manner of which is this. Therefore I am called Hermes Trismegistus <note>A legendary figure combining the Greek god Hermes and the Egyptian god Thoth; he was considered the patron of alchemy, which is often called the "Hermetic Art."</note>, having three parts of the philosophy of the whole world. <meta>This page continues Bernhard of Treviso's reflection on his failed alchemical experiments. On the previous page, he described his obsessive attempts to force nature and work with metals without true understanding. Here, he begins to articulate a theoretical realization: that ordinary "perfect" metals (like gold) cannot transform "imperfect" metals (like lead) through simple melting and mixing, because they lack surplus "perfection" to share.</meta>

# Second Part

->Bernhardi<-

...gold, but the lead vanishes from the mixture and is burnt away, while the gold truly remains in the examination; similarly, the remaining imperfect bodies also vanish. <note>original Latin: "bo aurum, sed evanescit plumbum ab amixtione, & aduritur, aurum verò in examinatione remanet: similiter & reliqua imperfecta corpora evanescunt." The "bo" is the completion of a word from the previous page.</note> (That is, metals indeed have a great and close relationship to one another, yet no perfect thing can perfect an imperfect thing, even if they are mixed together in a molten state. For if you let gold flow with lead and stir them together as well as possible, no gold will come from that same lead; instead, it flies away during the assaying <term>Probiren</term> <note>The process of testing the purity of a metal.</note> and burns up, but the gold remains on the cupel <term>Test</term> <note>A shallow, porous bowl used in assaying to separate precious metals from base metals.</note>; all other imperfect metals do the same.

For the perfect bodies <term>corpora perfecta</term>, those which are simply perfected by nature, are only "perfect" in their first degree. Unless they have become more-than-perfect <term>plusquamperfect</term> <note>A state where the substance has been concentrated or "multiplied" by alchemy to the point where it can share its quality with others.</note> through the Art, they can in no way assist the imperfect bodies <term>imperfecten Corporibus</term> (through mixing). This is because they possess no more perfection than is necessary for their own being <term>Esse</term> and essence. Since no one can give to another what they themselves cannot do without, that which is in need of help must remain so. It is as if one person (to use a crude comparison) were to give their skin to another; they would become just as miserable—indeed, far more miserable—than the person who asked it of them.

<meta>Catchword: un</meta>

<summary>Bernhard explains that ordinary gold cannot transform base metals like lead into gold through simple melting, as gold only possesses enough "perfection" for its own existence. He argues that for transmutation to occur, the "perfect" body must be raised to a "more-than-perfect" state through alchemy.</summary>

In the same way, if the perfect bodies <term>Corpora</term> <note>In alchemy, "bodies" refers to the metals themselves.</note> were to share their perfection with the imperfect ones without some intermediary means, they would be worth nothing and would be just as miserable as the imperfect bodies; for the perfect bodies, remaining as they do in their natural perfection, could in no way do such a thing, because they are like dead bodies.

To prove further that the imperfect bodies cannot be perfected by the perfect ones in this manner: it is certain that in a molten state <term>Fluß</term>, or through other deceptive tricks <term>Sophistischen Griffen</term> <note>The author uses "sophistical" to describe chemical operations that appear to work on the surface but do not achieve a true internal transformation.</note>, they can by no means be mixed and united at the most minute level <note>original Latin: *per minima misciret* and *uniret*</note>, and therefore one nature cannot come to the aid <note>original Latin: *succurriren*</note> of the other. **And even if the perfection of the noble metals could be mixed with the imperfect ones, the imperfect would not be perfected by the perfect, but rather the perfection of the noble ones would be diminished by the imperfect.** <note>original Latin: *Et, si esset commiscibilis nobilium metallorum perfectio cum imperfectis, non imperfecta cum perfectis perficerentur, sed eorum perfectio cum imperfectis diminueretur.*</note> (That is: even if the perfect, noble metals allowed themselves to be mixed with the imperfect, the imperfect would not be perfected by the perfect, but rather the perfection of the noble ones would be lessened by the imperfect.) That this cannot happen through melting alone, or in any other deceptive way outside of our Mastery <term>Magisterii</term> <note>The "Great Work" or the true process of creating the Philosopher's Stone.</note>, is something many philosophers have written about, as you will find in the *Pandects* <note>A term for a comprehensive compendium of knowledge.</note>, and the Book of GALID <note>Likely referring to the Arabic prince and alchemist Khalid ibn Yazid.</note>, as well as in the *Summa* of Geber <note>A reference to the *Summa Perfectionis*, one of the most famous alchemical texts of the Middle Ages, attributed to Geber (the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, though the text is likely by a 13th-century European author).</note>.

From these books, as I have recounted, I drew my foundation. *Nature is not improved, except within its own nature; nature contains and encompasses nature; nature separates nature; and nature, meeting its own nature, rejoices and is transformed into other natures.* <note>original Latin: *Natura emendatur, nisi in sua natura, natura naturam continet, natura naturam se-parat, & natura obvians naturæ suæ lætatur, & in alienas transmutatur naturas.* This is a fundamental alchemical axiom emphasizing that the "Great Work" must follow organic, natural laws rather than forced chemical reactions.</note>
<margin>The cause of nature.</margin>
(Nature is not improved, except in its own nature; nature holds and encompasses nature; nature separates nature; and nature rejoices in its own kind, and allows itself to be changed into another nature.) This philosophical **maxim** <term>dictum: a formal pronouncement or authoritative saying</term>, along with others I had now observed and found in the books, instructed me so greatly that I clearly recognized all the erroneous paths I had walked and abandoned them. Therefore, I studied even more industriously; I no longer wished to undertake anything "with the fist" <note>German: *mit der Faust*; an idiom meaning manual labor or brute-force experimentation performed without theoretical understanding.</note> until I had grasped the true foundation entirely. Thus, I did not sleep for many a night and pursued the matter most diligently, considering...

## Part Two

<margin>The philosophers agree on one thing.</margin>
Also, since I could obtain nothing true in this way (apart from Divine help) and realized that "no one else would show it to me," I thought: "he who knows it will not tell you, and he who does not know it cannot help you; therefore, let all men go in this regard, for all the expense you spend on anyone is lost." And for that reason, I once again left it to chance, then looked diligently at where the **philosophical books** <term>philosophical books: In this context, the author refers to the works of "the philosophers," the traditional term for master alchemists like Geber, Rhazes, or Hermes Trismegistus.</term> coincide. (*"Because where many agree, there we must adhere more closely."* Gratarolo <note>original Latin: *Quia ubi plures concordant, ibi debemus magis adhærere. Gratarol.* Refers to Guglielmo Gratarolo (1516–1568), an Italian physician who published influential collections of alchemical texts.</note>). I held that to be the truth, for they can say no truth except in one thing, since truth cannot be in many, but only in one. And in such a way I have come to the right path: For where I saw that they aimed most especially at one thing, that was precisely what I had sought so anxiously; and though one calls it by this name and another by another, it is nevertheless only one single **substance**, and the error lies only in the many and varied words and strange figures, and not in the **concordance** <note>original: *Concordanz*; the idea that beneath different terminologies, all true alchemists are describing the same natural process.</note>.

Therefore, dear reader, whoever comes across this book of mine, do not let such strange writing—which I produce not for my sake, but for yours—cause you wonder; for you can at least see therein what I worked upon and found nothing, so that you do not take up the same and come to harm, since an old <note>The text breaks off here; the catchword "Sprich-" indicates the next page begins with "Sprichwort" (proverb).</note>

<summary>Bernard explains his breakthrough: by comparing different alchemical texts, he realized that despite their confusing and varied language, the true masters all point toward a single, unified substance. He positions his writing as a cautionary guide to help others avoid the costly and fruitless experiments that consumed his own early years.</summary>

Particularly, they are those fellows who say their work is true, right, and certain without **philosophical reasons** <note>original Latin: *rationes Philosophicas*. # Bernhardi <note>original: "Bernhardi", the Latinized genitive form of Bernard, referring here to the works or sayings of Bernard of Trevisan.</note>

...they [imagine] themselves to be just as good, or even better than others; they make great **oaths** <term>oaths: From the German 'Schwür'; solemn vows or boasts intended to convince others of their expertise.</term>, and at times they snort and bluster at one who is devoted to the Art out of love, so that he must remain silent before them. For one must not anger such **fellows** <term>fellows: Translated from 'Gesellen', meaning journeymen or practitioners of a craft, used here disparagingly for charlatans.</term>; they would run into the **Rhine** <note>The Rhine river is used here as a hyperbolic and sarcastic metaphor for the practitioners' arrogance and perceived power.</note> and drown the world, which would indeed be possible [in their own minds].

However, just as all their work has a "foundation" and is "possible," so too is this drowning possible; for although the Rhine is not large enough for such a feat, there is at least water in it. Thus it is with the Art of these fellows as well: if the works themselves are not present, then there are at least proud, high words, which such fellows can deliver so scornfully that the heart of a poor fellow—who studies and must hear such loud-talkers while remaining silent—might break.

For only their lying, boastful words are believed, at least by those who do not know any better. But the advice of the poor fellow, who does not **babble** <note>original: "wäscht", literally "washes," but used idiomatically in this period to mean talking excessively or nonsensically.</note> much, yet has read and thought much, counts for nothing. Therefore, such treacherous villains float to the top and insist on being right above all others, whether it bends or breaks, whether it be true or not. Such **villainous tricks** <term>villainous tricks: From 'Bubenstück', referring to the fraudulent schemes and moral failings of dishonest alchemists.</term> pass as currency for the deceivers. But if a poor fellow, who studies and seeks the foundation and applies himself to the truth, should meet with failure, he then has the **devil in his hair** <note>A German idiom 'den Teuffel in Haaren', meaning to be in a state of great trouble, distress, or to be subject to harsh, relentless criticism.</note>. He must be called **Master Smarty-pants** <term>Master Smarty-pants: Translated from 'Meister Klügel', a mocking title for someone who thinks they are clever but is perceived as a fool or a pedant by others.</term>, who bridles the horse at the wrong end, and must...

## Part Two

Now these honor-forgetting **vagabonds** <term>vagabonds: Translated from 'Landbeschmeisser', a derogatory term for traveling charlatans who "defile the land" with their presence.</term> not only have the manner, but they also have the trick: when one wants to know what they are capable of, what they have worked on, or the nature of their **sophistical recipe** <term>sophistical recipe: A 'Sophistisch Recept' refers to a formula that sounds logical or "philosophical" but is intentionally misleading or false.</term>—from which one might see whether they are to be trusted or not—they **keep the porridge in their mouths** <note>original: "behalten sie den Brey im Maul." An idiom meaning to speak unclearly, mumble, or refuse to speak plainly to avoid commitment.</note>. They will not bark it out like dogs, but utter barely half-words, so that at times a single word one wants from them must be worth a **guilder** <term>guilder: From 'Gulden', a gold coin used as currency in the Holy Roman Empire.</term>. 

Yet they are not to be blamed for this; for since their purpose is to **deceive** <note>original: "aufzusetzen", meaning to hoodwink or impose upon someone.</note> people, they must remain silent so that they do not betray themselves and their **villainy** <term>villainy: From 'Bubenstück', literally a "boy's trick" or a rogue’s deed.</term> is noticed; for he who remains silent does not betray himself. To further confirm such fraud, they boast of certain learned men from whom they claim to have received their knowledge; they are **well-feathered** <note>Likely meaning they are well-prepared with false credentials or impressive appearances to look the part of a scholar.</note> and swear that if they did not share it out of loyalty, no soul would ever know of it. 

In this way, they cause many an honest man to let go of his own good thoughts—attained through reading many good books and his own diligence—to follow such **arrogant fools** <term>arrogant fools: From 'Hochdunckeln', referring to those puffed up with self-importance or "high-thinking" in a pejorative sense.</term> who cannot speak two words of **Latin** <note>Latin was the universal language of scholarship and alchemy; an inability to speak it was proof of a lack of genuine education.</note>, let alone anything else. Thus, through such fraud, the honest man comes to harm, ridicule, and disadvantage.

### Bernhardi.

[Ele]ments yield to the working of nature and leave her room to work the seed. <meta>This page continues the argument regarding the limitations of human "Art" (technology or alchemy) compared to "Nature." It builds on the previous page's point that Art cannot create the "seed" of life or matter, but must instead follow the blueprints provided by God-given Nature.</meta>

# Bernhardi <note>Likely referring to Bernhardus Trevisanus (1406–1490), a celebrated alchemist whose writings emphasized that the alchemist is merely a "servant" of nature.</note>

...[Art] is only a helper of nature, for where nature is not present, it can have no effect.

Just as if you wanted to administer a **laxative** <term>Laxatiff; a medicine used to stimulate the body to purge itself</term> to a dead man, you would accomplish nothing; for it would not purge—regardless of how much skill you applied to it—because nature is no longer there to receive it. Therefore, place **Art** after **Nature**, and do not expect it to do more than that nature, which GOD has given it, can do within itself. Since it is true that where nature does not work, art must also cease, what then is the use of the remaining labor?

<margin>Nature must create the **matter** <term>Materie; the physical substance or raw material for alchemical work</term></margin>
Therefore, it is necessary: where art is to work, it must begin from nature; and nature must create the **matter** <note>original: *Materiam*</note>, and not art. ## TREATISE
### of Bernhard, Count of Treviso <note>original Latin: *Bernhardi, Comitis Trevirensis*. Bernhard (1406–1490) was a famous Italian alchemist whose works were widely translated and studied during the Renaissance.</note>
### on the <term>Philosopher’s Stone</term> <note>The "Stein der Weisen," the legendary substance said to be capable of transmuting base metals into gold and achieving the "Great Work."</note>

Having perceived the desire and longing hope of those who practice the art of <term>Alchemy</term> <note>original: *Alchymiæ*; the medieval predecessor to chemistry, focused on the transmutation of matter and the perfection of the human soul.</note>, I wished in the present treatise to explain this same art briefly and publicly.

Therefore, one should first know what the art deals with; secondly, its foundation; thirdly, how one should proceed therein; and fourthly and finally, the extraction <note>Referring to the process of drawing out the essential spirit or tincture from the prepared material.</note>

The **Subject** <note>original: *Subjectum*; the base material or "Prime Matter" from which the work begins.</note> or the very thing with which this wonderful Art deals is **Gold and Silver**, or rather **Man and Woman**. The Man is warm and dry, but the Woman is cold and moist; and you should know for certain that our **Stone** is composed of no other thing. The **Process** <note>original: *Process*; the specific sequence of alchemical operations.</note> is nothing other than a work of contraries: for the description of contrary things is of one kind, and if you create such an equality twice, you will bring the whole process to its conclusion.

# Special Treatise

...are Sulphur and *Mercury* <note>original: *Mercurius*; in alchemy, these represent the "philosophical" principles of stability (Sulphur) and fluidity or spirit (Mercury) rather than common store-bought chemicals.</note>, which, because they are joined together, must be separated from one another and purified, so that they may afterwards be better mixed and reunited with the *body* from which they were first drawn.

Once the colors have passed away, and that which is above has become like that which is below, and that which is below has become like that which is above <note>This is a famous reference to the *Emerald Tablet*, a fundamental text of Hermeticism that describes the unity of the macrocosm (the universe) and the microcosm (the individual or the alchemical vessel).</note>, wonders will arise from it. When this has occurred, you will have a *triangle* within a *quadrangle*, and the fifth <note>The "Quintessence" (literally the "fifth essence"), a celestial substance that transcends the four physical elements of Earth, Air, Fire, and Water.</note>, which is contained within the four.

Now there remains the Multiplication <note>The final stage where the potency and quantity of the alchemical Stone are increased.</note>, about which this must be briefly noted: namely, that the *Elixir* should be nourished with the very things from which it was initially composed. No one among the *philosophers* <note>original: *Philosophis*; here meaning "alchemists," as alchemy was then considered a branch of natural philosophy.</note> before now has explained this as publicly as I have done in this place. This was done for two reasons: the first is that a long time is required from the beginning to the end of the Work, even though some *philosophers* say that the Stone can be completed in a single day, and others in a single month. You should know, however, that they speak figuratively, and their words must not be understood in that literal way. Nevertheless, I agree with *SCOTUS* <note>Likely Michael Scot (c. 1175–c. 1232), a legendary scholar and scientist often associated with alchemical and occult secrets in medieval tradition.</note> and say that the Stone, or the perfect Work, can be completed in a single year.

For this reason, I have explained everything here so clearly and publicly, so that this most noble science may not be lost or perish.

### His Theory <note>original: *Theorica ejusdem*</note>

But in the thing itself, these names are not distinct, because the matter is always one and the same alone, of one kind of material and always of one nature; to which nothing is added that has not been drawn out of it, being most closely related to it and of its own quality.

# Special Treatise

...pure and bright water, constant, pure and clear, of a celestial color. And if the water did not come to our medicine, it could not cleanse or improve itself; therefore you would not obtain your desire. 

But that which is improved is the gold, for without it the water cannot be improved; then without the gold and its shadow <note>original: *Schatten*; in alchemical theory, the "shadow" of gold often refers to its hidden, internal qualities or the impurities that must be refined to reach its spiritual essence.</note> the tinging medicine <note>original: *tingirende Arzney*; the Tincture or Elixir capable of "tinging" (transforming) base metals.</note> cannot be born. Now, whoever thinks the tincture could be made without these two bodies—namely, gold and silver—approaches the work as a blind man. 

For one body does not act upon another body, nor one spirit upon another. Neither does one form take shape from another, nor one matter <note>original: *Materia*</note> from another, because like does not act upon nor suffer from its like: because one is no more worthy than the other, and therefore no action can occur between them, since an equal has no command over its equal. 

Rather, the body receives a shape from the spirit, just as matter does from form, and the spirit from the body; for they are so made and created by God that one acts upon the other, and one suffers from the other. Indeed, the matter would flow infinitely if the form did not stop and still such flow. Therefore, because the body <note>original: *Corpus*</note> is its form that prepares the work, it gives the spirit its form and retains it, so that henceforth it can flow no further.

# Special Treatise of Bernhard

I give you the saying of MORIENUS <note>Morienus was a semi-legendary 7th-century alchemist known for his dialogue with King Khalid. His teachings emphasize the unification of the four elements.</note>, concerning the dissolution of Air, Earth, Fire, and Water. Some, when they speak of the dissolution, say the <term>Dissolution</term> <note>original: *Solutio*; the process of turning a solid substance into a liquid or primordial state.</note> of Fire is better, because whatever is dissolved in Fire vanishes into Air. And note, that the <term>Philosophers' Fire</term> <note>original: *Philosophorum Feuer*; a symbolic "secret" fire, not common fire, used to animate the matter.</note> is nothing other than a dissolved and re-hardened Air.

You can understand this better through an analogy: suppose that you first have the dissolved and re-hardened Air; to this, add the Fire. The Earth must be previously prepared, and the Fire <term>dissolved</term> <note>original: *solviret*</note>, before they are mixed together.

The Earth should also be placed together with the Fire into a suitable vessel, and thereafter one should bring into it the inextinguishable fire of the nuts <note>original: *Feuer der Nüsse*; likely referring to *ignis nucum*, a specific grade of heat produced by burning nut-sized coals or shells, providing a steady, moderate temperature.</note>, which, when it descends down upon the Earth, swallows it entirely with its <term>Gum</term> <note>original: *Gummi*; a technical term for the sticky, resinous state of the matter during the transformation process, often called "the gum of the Sages."</note>, and transforms it into its own nature. Therefore, if you rightly and well consider the sayings and teachings of the Sages, and understand their hidden meaning, you will come to all the secrets of the excellent art of <term>Alchemy</term> <note>original: *Alchimia*</note>.

To the Triune God, the eternal Creator, and overflowing fountain of grace, and Father of all wisdom, as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit in one Godhead, be

->eternity to eternity,<-

## To Master Thomas of Bologna, Personal Physician to Charles VIII, King of France.

A greeting and my most diligent service be with you, highly learned Doctor, dear friend, etc. I wish to inform you that I have duly received from Master Aldereich your long and extensive letter, together with the stone of your secret work; from this, I perceived a special sign of your good friendship toward me, and I have gathered enough from it to now be certain that you have unfailingly directed your high genius <term>Ingenium; innate talent or natural capacity for understanding complex truths</term> and sharp intellect [toward the goal]. Therefore, highly learned Doctor, every claim is false and void where it is taught to alter or change the **Mercury** <term>Mercury (Mercurium); the liquid metal quicksilver, considered by alchemists to be the "seed" or fundamental substance of all metals</term>, which is the seed, before joining the **metallic species** <note>original: *Metallischen Specierum*; referring to the specific types of metals being worked with</note> with it. # Count Bernhard’s [Chemical Writings]

...withdraws [the solvent], the **body** <term>Body (Corpus); the physical substance or "flesh" of a metal</term> can still be melted just as before. Such a water cannot remain with the **body**, nor can it be considered a moisture that belongs to it in its **root** <note>original: *Wurtzel*; the fundamental essence or natural origin of the metal</note>. The **bodies** <term>Bodies (Corpora)</term> are indeed **corroded** <term>Corroded (corrodirt); chemically eaten away by acid</term> and consumed, but they are not **dissolved** <term>Dissolved (solvirt); truly liquefied into their primary matter</term>. The more they are **corroded**, the further they are diverted and alienated from their **metallic species** <note>original: *Metallischen Specie*; the specific identity of the metal, such as gold or silver</note>.

Therefore, such **solutions** <term>Solutions (Solutiones)</term> have no foundation in the Art <note>The "Art" refers to Alchemy</note> of transforming metals. Instead, they are the deceptions of **sophists** <term>Sophists (Sophisten); here meaning charlatans or false teachers who use logic to hide their lack of practical success</term> and worthless alchemists who imagine that this worthy Art lies hidden in such things. 

They claim, nonetheless, that they are making **solutions**, but they will never make the **metallic species** perfect or complete. # Chemical Writings.

For in <term>Mercury</term> <note>In alchemy, Mercury represents the "feminine" principle of liquidity and coldness, consisting of Earth and Water.</note> there are two obvious acts, or visible <term>elements</term>, namely Water and Earth, which are called the passive or suffering <term>elements</term>. For this reason and cause, gold is dissolved with <term>Mercury</term> through the Art <note>The "Art" refers to the practice of Alchemy.</note>, so that the immature might be aided by the mature. Thus, as the Art cooks it and Nature perfects it, through the grace of God the <term>composition</term> is accomplished all the faster and sooner.

From this, one can now easily recognize and find the reason why, through the work of the <term>Philosophical Art</term> <note>The secret methods used by alchemists to replicate and accelerate natural processes.</note>, a nobler, more perfect, and higher grade of gold can be made much sooner and in a shorter time than can happen through the work of Nature.

# Count Bernard

For Nature does nothing else than digest and cook the single **Mercury**, by itself and alone, within the veins of the earth, without any further help or addition; therefore, it cannot so quickly reach the required *Proportion* and *Perfection* of gold or another *metal*. Our Art, however, assists the work of Nature by adding mature gold to the **Mercury**, which contains a very highly digested <term>Sulfur</term> <note>In alchemy, Sulfur represents the active, masculine principle of heat and dryness that "ripens" the cold, moist Mercury.</note>. This Sulfur very quickly matures the **Mercury** and digests it into the <term>anatical</term> <note>original: "Anatischen." Referring to a perfectly balanced or equalized ratio of elements.</note> and balanced *Proportion* of gold, by making the *Elements* of the **Mercury** increasingly subtle. Therefore, a truly wonderful shortcut of the natural work follows from this Art.

Consequently, dear Mr. *Doctor*, so that I may return to my purpose, one should not believe—as some err and fail in saying—that the active male seed is indeed added to the female seed during <term>coagulation</term> <note>The process where liquid components become solid or "fixed."</note> but is then separated from it again once the coagulation is complete. For as is known, in every <term>generation</term> <note>The alchemical term for the "birth" or creation of a new substance.</note> of a fruit of the womb or a child, there is an <term>active and passive</term> <note>original: "activum & passivum." Both the working and the suffering—that is, all four *Elements*—must remain together at all times; otherwise, no mixing could occur, nor could the birth of any fruit be hoped for.

But they finally find through experience that they have been deceived, and that such a thing is useless for our **Work** <note>Referring to the "Great Work" (Magnum Opus) of creating the Philosopher's Stone.</note>.

They can indeed change the **metallic forms** <note>original: "Metallische Species"</note> into the shape of an oil, but to bring them back into a metallic form so that the **proportion of the mixture** remains completely unbroken, they cannot. Nevertheless, such oil can be used as **medicine** <note>original: "Arzney"</note> for the human body, because the essence of gold has been dissolved within it; however, it certainly does not belong to our **Philosophical Work** and is unfit and useless for it. ### Count Bernard’s

The reason why things that are <term>homogeneous</term> <note>original: "Homogenea"; substances of a uniform nature or composition throughout.</note>, or of a uniform nature, possess a permanent and stable <term>fixation</term> <note>original: "Fixion"; the alchemical process of making a volatile substance stable and resistant to heat.</note>.

Those who believe they can extract a clear, transparent, and translucent water from mercury in such a manner, and achieve many wonders with it, are greatly mistaken.

...[of metals] King and Head, <note>original: "metallorum Rex & Caput"</note> which neither earth corrupts, nor burning fire consumes, nor water kills or devours, because its substance is fixed, and its nature is balanced in heat, moisture, cold, and dryness, and within it there is nothing superfluous or lacking. <margin>104.</margin> Inwardly, the words say this: Gold in its interior is spiritual, celestial, astral, volatile, fiery, airy, and watery; it is black, white, red, and of all colors, and altogether equal <note>original: "omninò æquale"</note> to all elements.

# Count Bernard’s #

...perfectly reached its goal, it stops working; for in gold lies the end of the entire natural operation. Therefore, the philosophers seek and find the secrets of nature in nothing else but gold, which is why they also call gold the finality and perfection of all metals. Thus, **BERNHARDUS** <note>Count Bernard of Trevisan, a 15th-century alchemist</note> intends that nature has inscribed the power and virtue into the gold (or "golden booklet") as into the <term>Matter of the Stone|the raw material required to create the Philosopher's Stone</term> <note>original: "Materiam Lapidis"</note> and has preserved it as a great treasure. However, nature cannot bring it forth by itself; therefore, she has publicly displayed the gold as perfectly as she has prepared and hung it out. 

In the other minerals and metals, however, this perfection is still hidden, invisible, and unprepared; therefore, nature still holds them under her obedience and operation, and has not yet fashioned, qualified, prepared, or publicly displayed them. For this reason, the **PHILOSOPHER** wishes that one should leave all other things of nature alone and take nothing except that which she has already prepared and displayed.

**Albert.** But to whom did the Old Man display the booklet?

**Georg.** To no one but the <term>Philosophical Community|the collective body of those learned in the alchemical arts</term> <note>original: "Facultati Philosophicæ"</note>.

**Albert.** But why?

**Georg.** Because no one can understand such a secret except the philosophers alone.

<summary>This page explains that gold represents the "finality" of nature's work, where all elemental operations cease because perfection has been reached. Because of this, alchemists (the "Philosophical Community") believe that the secrets of the Philosopher's Stone are hidden within gold itself rather than in "unprepared" base metals.</summary>

**Albert.** But you did say that the <term>Philosophical Faculty|the collective body of those learned in the alchemical arts</term> <note>original: "Facultas Philosophiæ"</note> is the Art itself.

**Georg.** Yes, quite right; for even the philosophers, without their Art—and especially that which nature requires—are not able to win this jewel through their disputation <note>In this context, a "disputation" is a formal academic debate or a logical defense of a theory</note> alone. Nor does the wise man, nor the <term>Faculty</term>, entrust it to any other except those who have studied such an Art and are experienced and well-practiced in it. And for that reason, the philosopher **BERNHARD** <note>Count Bernard of Trevisan, a 15th-century alchemist known for his long search for the Stone</note> also says that he did not set himself to this disputation until he felt himself to be skilled enough.

**Albert.** Why did Bernard alone obtain the golden jewel?

**Georg.** Because, as he says, he disputed about the Art in the best and most skillful manner.

**Albert.** But did the others not dispute as well as he did?

**Georg.** No, for in their disputation of the Art they are not only very inconsistent, but they are also completely contrary to one another, and above all, they are entirely opposed to nature and Art.

**Albert.** How does that happen?

**Georg.** Because they are not of one mind with nature and Art. For some held inconsistent and opposing opinions regarding the <term>Matter|the raw material required to create the Philosopher's Stone</term> <note>original: "Materia"</note>, some regarding the <term>Composition|the process of combining alchemical ingredients</term>, some regarding the <term>Dissolution|the process of breaking a substance down into its primary components</term> <note>original: "Auflösung"</note>, some regarding the entire preparation; some sought the Stone in herbs such as <term>Moonwort|a fern traditionally associated with the moon and silver</term> <note>original: "Lunaria"</note>, and some in animals, such as in blood,

From all of this, you clearly see in brief what his dispute was and how he prepared himself for it. **Alb.** Tell me one thing, however: how can one prove that there is a different <term>Sulphur|the alchemical principle of "soul," fire, or combustibility</term> and <term>Mercurius|the alchemical principle of "spirit," liquidity, or volatility</term> in <term>Venere|Venus, the alchemical name for Copper</term> <note>original: "Venere"</note>, another in <term>Luna|the Moon, the alchemical name for Silver</term> <note>original: "Luna"</note>, and another in <term>Saturno|Saturn, the alchemical name for Lead</term> <note>original: "Saturno"</note>, and that each brings forth its own kind?

When one joins Mercury and Copper together in a skillful and proper manner, the Sulfur of Copper changes the Mercury into Copper; likewise, the Sulfur of Silver changes the Mercury into Silver. As <term>Gratianus|a speaker in the "Turba Philosophorum," an early alchemical assembly text</term> says in the *Turba*:
> "Every metal is in Mercury; therefore, whatever you sow in it, that you shall also reap from it." <note>original: "Omne Metallum est in Mercurio, unde quale semines in eum, tale & metes ex eo."</note>

And <term>Richardus Anglicus|Richard of England, a 13th-century alchemist</term> in his *Correctorium*, chapter 15:
> "Nature rejoices in its own nature, and not through some other foreign medium—namely, Gold with Gold, Silver with Silver, Copper with Copper, and so with the others—because each one transmits its own power into it." <note>original: "Natura congaudet suæ naturæ, & non per aliud medium extraneum, scilicet cum Sole Sol, cum Luna Luna, cum Venere Venus, & sic de aliis, quia unumquodque mittit in illum vim suam."</note>

**Alb.** What is the debate, then, concerning the jewel or the "little golden book"?

**Georg.** This debate is nothing other than the secret exploration of the natures of things—specifically, how one might dissolve the firm <term>Conjunction|the chemical union or binding of elements</term> and the cohesion of the elements, or those bonds of natural unity that exist within gold or the "little golden book." <note>The "little golden book" refers to the core principles of alchemical transformation often hidden in allegorical texts.</note>

It is for this very reason, says **BERN.**, that we reduce it from its metallic body into <term>Sperma|the "seed" or primal, fluid state of matter from which all things grow</term>. Without this reduction, the *Philosophers' Stone* <note>original: "Lapis Philosophorum"</note> cannot be made. And he speaks yet again—

**Georg.** But have you not also read that **BERNHARDUS** <note>Bernhard of Treviso (1406–1490), a famous Italian alchemist who reportedly spent his life and fortune seeking the Philosopher's Stone.</note> says in his *Letter to Thomas of Bologna* <note>Thomas of Bologna was a physician to King Charles V of France and a correspondent of Bernhard.</note> that this dissolution through <term>Aquafort|Nitric acid, commonly used by goldsmiths to separate metals.</term> is not a true Philosophical Work or <term>Solution|Solutio; the process of liquefying a solid metal so its "seeds" can be released.</term>, but rather a <term>Destruction|Destructio; the argument that harsh acids ruin the metallic nature rather than perfecting it.</term>? He further states: "Thus, however, the **Sophists** <note>A derogatory term used by alchemists to describe those who work blindly with chemistry without understanding natural philosophy.</note> think they are dissolving, wandering away from nature, but they do not dissolve," <note>original: "Sic tamen Sophistæ solvere se putant, in natura errantes, sed non solvunt"</note> and continues: "Bodies are indeed corroded, but they are not dissolved; and the more they are corroded, the more they are alienated from their metallic species. Therefore, solutions of this kind are not the foundation of the transmuting art, but rather the deceptions of Sophistical Alchemists, who think that this sacred art lies hidden in these things." <note>original: "Corpora quidem corroduntur, sed non solvuntur, & quantò magis corroduntur, tantò magis à metallica specie alienantur. **Georg.** My dear Albert, you are not yet sufficiently informed of the Philosophers' meaning in these matters, for **PETRUS BONUS FERRARIENSIS** <note>An Italian alchemist known for his work "The Precious New Pearl" (Margarita Pretiosa Novella), written around 1330.</note> says in the 10th chapter of his *New Pearl*: "For the Philosophers wrote these things with the cunning of parables, saying one thing and meaning another, so that they might lead the foolish astray and separate them from the truth; and those who do not understand work only according to the literal sound of the writing, and in the end they find no truth and are amazed; and then, believing they are acting well, they change these recipes and multiply and extend them to infinity. The Philosophers, however, [mean] only one..." <note>original: "Scripserunt enim Philosophi hæc cum versutiis parabolarum, unum dicentes & aliud intelligentes, ut fatuos seducant, & a vero sequestrent, & ii non intelligentes, operantur juxta sonum scripturæ tantùm, & in fine nil veritatis reperiunt, & mirantur: & post credentes benè agere, has receptiones mutant, & in infinitum multiplicant & extendunt. Philosophi autem unum tantum"</note>

Here you see that **Bernhard** <note>Bernhard of Treviso (1406–1490) was a celebrated alchemist who argued that the secret solvent of the philosophers must be made from the same substance as the metals themselves.</note> sets down three things which the **Philosophical water** should have:

First, it should be from the **root of the metals**.

Secondly, it should remain permanent and constant with the metals, both in **matter** and **form** <note>In the Aristotelian science of the time, "matter" was the physical substance, while "form" was the internal essence that made a thing what it was.</note>.

Thirdly, it should at the same time **coagulate** <note>Change from a liquid to a solid state.</note> with the dissolved metals. This, he says, cannot happen with **strong waters** <note>original: "Aquis fortibus"; this refers to corrosive mineral acids like nitric acid, which dissolve metals but do not "unite" with them in the alchemical sense.</note>, for first, they are not the root and the foundation of the metals.

Fourthly, they do not remain permanent and constant in the ground-root of the metal, for in **distilling**, they leave the **bodies** <note>The metallic substance.</note> lying **at the bottom** <note>original: "in fundo"</note> and separate from them through the **alembic** <note>A piece of laboratory glassware used for distillation.</note> and the heat of the fire; therefore, as stated in the third point, they cannot at the same time **coagulate** in the dissolution with the bodies.

From all this it now clearly appears that **nitric acid** <note>original: "Aquafort"</note>, **spirit of wine** <note>original: "Spiritus vini"; concentrated alcohol.</note>, **vinegars** <note>original: "Aceti"</note>, and other oils and juices do not belong to the **Philosophical Solution**, nor are they the essential and actual true fountain in the **Parable of Bernhard**.

But hear what **ROSARIUS** <note>Referring to the *Rosarium Philosophorum* (The Rose Garden of the Philosophers), a highly influential alchemical text first printed in 1550.</note> says of this fountain, as he has painted it for our eyes in vivid color, as it were, such that it is **Solar, Lunar, and Mercurial** <note>Relating to the three primary alchemical principles or the metals gold (Sun), silver (Moon), and mercury (Mercury).</note>.

**Albert.** But how am I to understand what he says—that the stone was surrounded by an old oak tree?

**When I, after much study, felt myself a little [weary].** By this, it is indicated that he finally became weary of the vain, sophistical <term>dabbling</term><note>The author uses the word *Sudeln*, implying messy, unscientific, or "false" alchemical experiments conducted by those who do not understand the true principles.</note>, searching, and speculating, and had grasped the right foundation for philosophical knowledge. He was then prepared to proceed to the true Work: to continue on to win the "golden little book." That is to say, he had drawn the Mercury from the best and finest philosophical gold, prepared it in the "Indies" <note>In alchemical literature, "the Indies" or "the East" often symbolically refers to a specific stage of the process or a state of high purity and heat.</note>, and completed the first part of the philosophical Work—which is the <term>Solution</term> <note>Solution is the process of dissolving a solid substance into a liquid state, often the first major step in creating the Philosopher's Stone.</note>—by the help of the moist-vaporous fire. At that point, he became weary of studying and found the "Little Fountain" in a single night. This "night" signifies the vaporous and philosophical fire; for when a thing is meant to dissolve and grow, one says: "Oh, when the warm nights come, it will grow quickly," just as experience testifies that the nightly warmth...

because it, mixed with the moisture of the dew, visibly brings forth all things. Thus Bernhardus also says that in one night—that is, in the humid, warm fire through which the <term>Solution of Mercury</term><note>original Latin: *Solution Mercurii*; the process of dissolving the metallic principle into a liquid state.</note> occurred—he found the <term>Fountain</term><note>original Latin: *Fontinam*.</note>.

<margin>B. Tree-base</margin>
And he says further, it is surrounded by a white round stone; this signifies the <term>Physical Egg</term><note>original Latin: *Ovum Physicum*; the hermetically sealed glass vessel, often egg-shaped, where the alchemical transformation takes place.</note>. It is also surrounded by an old hollow oak tree split down the middle—that is, a high oaken sphere, cut in half, inside of which the glass [vessel] is meant to stand. This [sphere] must be full of holes at the bottom and not at the top, so that the vaporous fire can act upon the glass; and it is walled around, which signifies the furnace in which everything is properly arranged. He would have liked to sleep because he was tired from studying—that is, to rest and refresh himself—and he sat down by the fountain to watch; this is when the <term>Conjunction</term><note>The stage where the "male" and "female" principles of the matter are joined together.</note> would begin. There he sees the fountain open up at the top; that is, the <term>Oil</term><note>original German: *Oleum*; refers here to the refined, viscous essence of the matter.</note> being born from the fountain, so that it begins to gather at the top. Now everything had been at the bottom of the fountain, so that which was lowest raised itself up, and that which was highest lowered itself; and yet it was nevertheless enclosed. This is so that during the rising and falling, the fountain would not be diminished in its weight. And thus he sees the motion of rising and falling within the fountain, particularly the beginning of the thickening and <term>Oiliness</term><note>original German: *Olietat*; the transition of the substance into a fatty or oily consistency.</note>, and subsequently the little fibers and leaves, which he calls the <term>King in the Bath</term><note>A classic alchemical image representing a substance being dissolved or purified in a liquid medium, often preceding its "rebirth" or solidification.</note>.

### Count Bernhard’s ###

That he further asks the old priest about the circumstances of the **Fountain** and of the **King**, and receives his report or answer regarding this, is to be understood as follows. Because the fountain opens up, the King must have been in the fountain from the very beginning; and even if the fountain has already dried up, it nevertheless retains the name. And this **King in the Fountain**—that is, the <term>Sulfur</term><note>original Latin: *Sulphur*; the active, "combustible" male principle in alchemy, representing heat and soul.</note> hidden within the <term>Mercury of the Sun</term><note>original Latin: *Mercurio Solis*; a refined, philosophical mercury associated with gold.</note>—must therefore have the fountain (which comes from its own <term>Mercury</term><note>The fluid, "metallic" principle.</note>) necessarily sealed. This is so that during the <term>Solution</term><note>original Latin: *Solution*; the process of dissolving the solid matter into a liquid state.</note> nothing evaporates, which would otherwise be lacking later during the <term>Coagulation</term><note>original Latin: *Coagulation*; the thickening or solidifying of the dissolved matter.</note>.

It also indicates the form of the fountain: it is as clear as fine silver and of heavenly colors. It contains the **Mercurial Water**, through which it becomes even stronger; that is, when the <term>Solution of Mercury</term><note>original Latin: *Solutio Mercurii*.</note> has occurred in its own water and <term>Fountain</term><note>original Latin: *Fontina*.</note>, and the **Coagulation** and <term>Fixation</term><note>original Latin: *Fixation*; the process of making a substance stable under heat so it no longer evaporates.</note> begin, the fire must be strengthened by one degree by means of the oaken sphere. This is done to "protect the sun and its shine"—that is, to preserve the dry warmth hidden or locked within the <term>White Stone</term><note>The stage of the Great Work that produces silver; the matter has reached a state of stability and purity.</note>.

The marvelous nature of the fountain—how it ignites and rages so that it would penetrate everything—signifies the moment it becomes fire-red. This is a sign of its <term>Perfection</term><note>original Latin: *Perfection*; the final attainment of the alchemical Goal or the Red Stone.</note> and completeness. However, if it were to escape—that is, if the glass [vessel] were to break during the **Solution** while the matter is still <term>volatile</term><note>original Latin: *volatilis*; easily vaporized or evaporated.</note> and <term>spiritual</term><note>original German: *ſpiritualiſch*; referring to the matter being in a gaseous or vaporous state.</note>—we would be...

# CONCERNING THE GREAT PHYSICAL STONE.
<note>original: "DE MAGNO LAPIDE PHYSICO"</note>

->Concerning the<-

# Two Little Flowers /
## From which the Philosophers' Stone grows.

Once I was greatly troubled that I and others in the true and natural and nearly Divine art of **ALCHEMY** <note>original: "ALCHYMIA"; the medieval precursor to chemistry, aimed at the transformation of matter and the soul</note>, in so many years have been unable to experience or obtain anything certain, and so I stood in doubt whether the Almighty wished to let us poor sinners know this in this state of life. In such contemplation <note>original: "Speculation"; a term for deep study and meditation on the mysteries of nature</note> of mine, it happened that I was traveling and encountered a man on a mountain in the guise of a **peasant**, who supported himself on the mountain by the labor of his hands. This same peasant held in his hand **two little flowers**, one of the male sex, the other of the female sex, and of two different natures. I asked the peasant what he intended to do with the flowers? For I knew them both, but I did not know that they were of the male and female sex, or of two different colors. Then the peasant revealed to me that the flowers were tru-

-ly possessed the **Prime Matter** <note>original: "Primam Materiam"; the fundamental, formless substance from which all things originate in alchemy</note> within them, from which the great **Stone of the Philosophers** <note>original: "Stein der Philoſophorum"</note> is made, and could still be made with the help of **GOD**.

At this I marveled greatly, that from such a humble plant so highly important a stone could be made, and through simple **preparation** <note>original: "Præparation"</note>; and even greater was the wonder that the work should be so plain and simple that a peasant might understand it. It gladdened my heart that before my end I had seen a man who could possess and understand such a treasure. Therefore, I took counsel with myself on how the matter might be approached, so that I might learn the right **preparation** of this Stone, and something more. But all my thoughts and **contemplation** <note>original: "Speculation"</note> were ultimately anxious, for the matter was so highly important that reasonably no one should or can desire it. Therefore, I said to the peasant with a sigh:

## Count Bernhard’s

...would be a single thing—that is, of male and female gender—which are reckoned as one body. It is so common that even the poor possess it more than the rich; this is to be understood in the sense that these flowers are plucked by the poor and brought to the rich for their pleasure in exchange for money <note>This refers to the common alchemical trope that the "Materia Prima" or starting material is something humble, cheap, and overlooked by the worldly.</note>. I asked further who heated the **sweat-bath** <term>Schweißbad; a vessel providing gentle, indirect heat, often using water, ash, or sand to mimic the warmth of a womb</term>, and whether it had to be heated by some artful means? At this he laughed and said, "I use my farmhand for that, or a goose-herd, or a maid—it is all the same. For the furnace for this **sweat-bath** is so constructed that they cannot easily make the fire too strong or spoil anything within it. It remains at a certain constant heat, just as required, so that even a hen’s egg might be hatched therein." The reason he gave me was quite rational <note>Alchemists often compared the "digestion" of their substances to the natural incubation of an egg.</note>.

Finally, I asked if there were no other flowers besides those that possessed such great virtues. The peasant told me that there were six flowers of the male gender, and only one single kind of the female gender in the entire world. These he laid before me and said that from any of the male ones—if the female were added—a **Philosopher’s Stone** <term>Stein der Philosophen; the legendary substance of the "Great Work" capable of transmuting metals</term> could be made in the manner described. Each begets its own kind. He explained the reasons to me in detail, and they, too, were rational.

# Chemical Writings

<meta>catchword: I</meta>

## To the Reader

Favorable reader, you will remember, as was previously mentioned, that the four books of **Bernhard** <note>Count Bernhard of Trevisan (1406–1490), a legendary figure in alchemy who reportedly spent his life and fortune seeking the Philosopher’s Stone.</note> were written in the French language, and were first translated from that into the Latin language by **Gratarolus** <note>Guglielmo Gratarolo (1516–1568), an Italian physician who compiled and translated many important alchemical works.</note>. However, it has come into my hands that this is said to be the beginning of the fourth book in that same language, which I also wished to share with you, so that this work might come to light in a complete manner.

->Farewell <note>original: "Vale"</note><-

->J. T. C.<-

# Count Bernhard’s

I was tired from writing and studying. And there was an old castle or citadel, wherein dwelt two dragons; one was red and heavy of body, and the other was white and without wings. They came together and embraced each other in the heat of the sun when it is in **Aries** <note>original: "Ariete." The zodiac sign of the Ram, representing the beginning of spring and the traditional starting point of the alchemical Great Work.</note>, and they played together so long until the joined dragons lost their individual forms and changed together into a **black raven** <note>The "Raven’s Head" or *corvus* is a famous alchemical symbol for the stage of *nigredo* (blackness), signifying the death and decay of the matter before its purification.</note>. These moistened one another until they became as white as snow in the heat of the sun as it enters **Taurus** <note>The zodiac sign of the Bull.</note>, continuing until the sun entered **Leo** <note>The zodiac sign of the Lion; this progression through the zodiac signifies the increasing "heat" and maturation of the alchemical substance.</note>. Thus the raven, which had become white, eventually became red like blood in the heat, and in this work, it changed into a **Conjunction** <term>Conjunction; the "chemical wedding" or union of the opposing principles (often sulfur and mercury, or sun and moon).</term>, and it called itself the richest in the world.

At this I was terrified and intended to leave the orchard, but then I found a **fountain** <term>Fontin; an archaic term for a fountain. In this context, it refers to the "Philosophical Fountain" or the solvent used to "wash" the metallic matter.</term> very firmly walled in, which was guarded by an old wise man. I asked him to whom this well-protected fountain belonged. I was answered: "This aforementioned King, well known in these lands, comes from the fountain, and he nevermore leaves the fountain; he is afterward dried by the fountain, in which he then remains to bathe for 282 days, or ten and a half months <note>The period of 282 days correlates roughly to the human gestational period, a common alchemical metaphor for the "birth" of the Philosopher’s Stone.</note>. Through this, the King becomes so highly unified and rejuvenates himself that no one may overcome him."

### Chemical Writings. 295

Therefore the King made the fountain himself, and at first, he rests in a white, clear, and translucent stone, resting therein as clear as **Moon** <term>Luna; the alchemical name for Silver.</term> sky-blue. And so that no animal should come into it and gnaw upon it, a hollow oak is cut round through the middle <note>The "hollow oak" is a traditional alchemical metaphor for the furnace or the protective casing around the glass vessel.</note>, and that protects it and creates the heat of the sun. Likewise, on the outside, **Venus’s Hat** <term>Venus Hut; likely referring to a copper lid or the cooling hood of the vessel (alembic), as Venus is the planetary symbol for Copper.</term> is enclosed within thick walls. The fountain is well-guarded because it is of such wonderful powers and natures; this is so that it does not leak through or break open from the heat, for otherwise, we would be utterly lost if the fountain were to run dry. 

I asked, "Have you seen the King?" 
Answer: "Yes, I have seen him enter, but I have not seen him since his entrance. He keeps himself enclosed and does not show himself for one hundred and thirty-five days. After that, he begins to reveal himself and appear, white as snow, while the **Gatekeeper** <term>Pförtner; the "Porter" or "Gatekeeper" in alchemy usually represents the fire-tender or a chemical salt that "opens" the metals.</term> serves him and warms his bath constantly to preserve his natural heat, hidden in his clear water as was previously described; this bath is maintained day and night." 

Then I asked him, "What is the King’s clothing like?" 
He answered, "A coat of beaten gold, and a doublet black as velvet, and his shirt white as snow, and his body blood-red as blood." <note>These colors—black (nigredo), white (albedo), and red (rubedo)—are the three primary stages of the alchemical "Great Work," leading to the final "Gold."</note>

And there was an old castle or fortress, in which lived two dragons, one red and heavy of body, and the other white and without wings; and they came together and embraced each other in the heat of the sun, as it is in **Aries** <note>original: "Ariete"; the first sign of the zodiac, marking the beginning of the alchemical spring or process.</note>, and they played together until the joined dragons lost themselves and changed together into a **black raven** <term>The Black Raven (Corvus) represents the 'nigredo' or putrefaction stage, where the matter dies and turns black.</term> which moistened one another until they became white as snow in the heat of the sun, as it enters **Taurus** <note>original: "Taurum"; the second zodiac sign.</note>, until the sun came into **Leo** <note>original: "Leonem"; the sign of the Lion, associated with the completion of the work or the fixed state.</note>, so that the raven, which had become white, had become red at the last, like blood, in the heat; and it changed in this work into a **union** <term>Conjunction; the mystical joining of opposites, often personified as a royal marriage.</term> <note>original: "Conjunction"</note>, and he called himself the richest in the world. 

At this I was frightened and intended to leave the garden, but I found a **fountain** <note>original: "Fontin"</note> very firmly walled in, and it was guarded by an old wise man, whom I asked to whom the fountain belonged, which was so well guarded. Then it was answered to me: this aforementioned King, well-known in these lands, is of the fountain, and he never leaves the fountain, and is afterward dried by the fountain, in which he then remains to bathe for 282 days, or ten half-months; thereby the King becomes so highly unified and rejuvenates himself, that no one may overcome him.

### Chemical Writings

<meta>catchword: Therefore</meta>

Therefore the King made the fountain himself, and first rests within a white, clear, and transparent stone, resting within it as clear as **the Moon** <note>original: "Luna"; in alchemy, this refers to silver or the 'white' stage of the process.</note> sky-blue; and so that no animal should enter and gnaw upon it, a hollow oak is cut round through the middle, which guards it and creates the heat of the sun; likewise, on the outside, the **Cover of Venus** <note>original: "Venus Hut"; likely referring to a copper vessel or lid that seals the apparatus.</note> is closed in thick walls. The fountain is well-protected because it is of wondrous powers and natures, so that it does not penetrate through nor open itself up from the heat; otherwise, we would be entirely lost if the fountain were to run out. I asked: Have you seen the King? Answer: Yes, I have seen him enter, but I have not seen him since his entrance; he remains enclosed and does not allow himself to be seen for one hundred and thirty-five days. Thereafter he begins to reveal and manifest himself, as white as snow; meanwhile, the **Gatekeeper** <term>The Gatekeeper (Pförtner) often personifies the external heat of the furnace or a chemical agent that regulates the internal environment.</term> serves him and constantly warms his bath to preserve his natural heat, hidden in his clear water, as is prescribed; this bath is maintained day and night. Then I asked him: What is the King’s clothing? He answered: a robe of beaten gold, a **doublet** <note>original: "Wammes"; a close-fitting jacket common in the Renaissance.</note> as black as velvet, a shirt as white as snow, and his body as **sanguine-red** <note>original: "sanguinroth"</note> as blood.

## Of Gallus Etschenreuter /
->Doctor of <term>Medicine <note>original: "Artzney"</note></term> and Chemist, appointed <term>Physician <note>original: "Physici"; referring to the "Physicus," a publicly appointed communal doctor.</note></term> at Sélestat, written to<-
## Guglielmo Gratarolo /

Honorable and highly learned Doctor, gracious Lord and friend: the friendship and well-inclined will of the Lord <note>The author addresses Gratarolo respectfully as "the Lord" throughout, a common formal style in the 16th century.</note> toward me has so bound me to him that I cannot at all neglect—indeed, I am almost compelled—to love and honor the Lord in return, because he shows himself to be a distinguished patron and promoter of this art of <term>Alchemy <note>original: "Alchimey"</note></term> and proves it in deed. For your diligence, labor, and effort are directed solely toward ensuring that posterity understands that the Lord has lived gloriously in this world, or rather, so that his name shall not die but remain as long as the world stands. For you have earned great and glorious merit regarding <term>medicine <note>original: "Artzney"</note></term>, because you promote it so that it may be fruitful for the general benefit.

enough written, and that it rests upon the fact that the *Matter* <note>original Latin: "Materia"</note> of the **Philosopher’s Stone** is a twofold *Mercury* <note>original Latin: "Mercurius"</note>: one common, and one that is made from the metals. # Epistle
<meta>catchword: This</meta>

An analogy can be found in the leaven <note>original: "Sauerteig"; alchemists often compared their "Stone" or catalyst to yeast or leaven that transforms a larger mass of dough</note> and the whole dough from which bread is baked. Thus should the weight of common *Mercury* be in proportion to the Metallic *Mercury*.

Concerning the third point, I hold that these two alone are not sufficient for our work, for these reasons: because of the Holy Trinity—that God is triune, wood is triune, metal is triune. Thus **ARISTOTLE** <note>Aristotle's theory of the elements was fundamental to alchemy, though he posited four elements; the "three principles" mentioned here are a later adaptation</note> posits three primary things, and the German **THEOPHRASTUS** <note>Referring to Theophrastus von Hohenheim, known as Paracelsus (1493–1541), who established the "Tria Prima" (Sulfur, Mercury, and Salt) as the three fundamental components of all matter</note> demonstrates this clearly, and I have seen and experienced this myself in several different things. 

And this moves me especially: that noble Alchemists have held discussions about this—that when *Mercury* is coagulated <note>original: "coaguliret"; the process of turning a liquid into a solid or semi-solid state</note> and hardened, they said one could not bring it into a liquid state, nor would it become malleable enough to be hammered. Whether they understood this to mean common *Mercury*, or that which is made from metal, has slipped my mind. Indeed, I have personally, as you know, spoken with you about the *coagulation* of *Mercury*, and have partly dealt with it in writings, and will, when opportunity arises, *confer* <note>original: "conferiren"; to discuss or compare findings</note> further with you. 

This I must confess: that with gold and silver lime <note>original: "Kalch" (Calx); a powder produced by heating a metal, essentially its oxide</note>, I have *coagulated* one part of the *Mercury of Saturn* <note>original: "Mercurii Saturni"; in alchemy, Saturn is the symbol for Lead</note> so that it was malleable and could be cast; more than this I did not experience at that time.

# Gallus Etschenreuter

This third point cannot be thoroughly understood from **BERNHARD** <note>original: "Bernhardo"; likely referring to Bernhardus Trevisanus, a 15th-century alchemist famous for his work on the "Great Work" or the Philosopher's Stone</note>. If you had not set yourself so vehemently against **THEOPHRASTUS** <note>Theophrastus von Hohenheim, known as Paracelsus (1493–1541). He was a controversial figure who revolutionized medicine and chemistry by emphasizing minerals and chemicals over traditional herbal humor-based medicine</note>, who is a special ornament and honor to all of Germany, speaking of divine things <note>original Greek: "θειοφράζοντα" (theiophrázonta); a wordplay on the name Theophrastus, suggesting his words were divinely inspired</note> in Chemistry, having described almost divine things in Alchemy, I would have immediately revealed it to you, given you to understand, and proven from this author which metals it must be made from. 

Rather, you should—as it surprises me that you do not—set yourself against the false Paracelsians, or those who withhold his books (which are written so clearly and openly) and bury them for themselves. You are well aware that in **ARISTOTLE** there is a great difference between knowledge <note>original Greek: "ἐπιστήμην" (epistemen); theoretical or scientific knowledge</note> and the labor of knowledge <note>original Greek: "τὸν πόνον ἐπιστήμης" (ton ponon epistemes); the practical application or "work" required to gain or use science</note>. **THEOPHRASTUS** teaches in his books published so far the right use of medicine, namely, *knowledge*—the true science of remedies. Whether you wish to or not, you must confess that these were previously unknown to you, such as those against the severe ailments of <term>gout</term> <note>original: "Zipperlein"; a historical term for painful joint swelling, often gout</note>, <term>dropsy</term> <note>original: "Wassersucht"; an archaic term for edema or swelling caused by fluid accumulation</note>, and <term>leprosy</term> <note>original: "Aussatz"</note>. 

It is more fitting that we love such persons for their art, rather than hating or envying them because of certain human failings and weaknesses. Search your own heart: if you were to know what **THEOPHRASTUS** knew, would you reveal it? You would surely be acting against the oath <note>original Latin: "Juramentum"; referring to the Hippocratic Oath or the secret oaths taken by alchemists to protect their knowledge from the unworthy</note>...

# Missive

<meta>catchword: It</meta>

**HIPPOCRATES** <note>Ancient Greek physician (c. 460 – 370 BC) often regarded as the father of medicine; here he is cited as an authority on professional secrecy</note>, who does not want medicine to be revealed to everyone. Thus you know what happened in Bologna <note>original: "Bononien"</note>, that a man was condemned by a judgment and accused as a traitor to the fatherland, and even sentenced to the gallows, because for the first time he set up the instrument by which silk is artificially spun in Germany at Trent <note>original: "Trident"</note>. The Bolognese, as their Palace <note>original: "Palatium"</note> testifies, desired nothing more than to have torn off his head.

And even if you knew the **Philosopher’s Stone** <note>original: "Stein der Weisen"; the legendary substance capable of turning base metals into gold and granting eternal life</note> (than which there is nothing higher after **GOD** in this world, as the **Senior** <note>original: "Senior"; refers to Senior Zadith, the Latinized name of the 10th-century Arabic alchemist Ibn Umayl</note> writes in the *Counsel on the Marriage of the Sun and Moon* <note>original Latin: "Consilio conjugii Solis & Lunæ"; a foundational alchemical text describing the union of solar/sulfuric and lunar/mercurial principles</note>) and wished to make it public, then you would not be a son or disciple of **HERMES** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom the "Hermetic" secret sciences of alchemy and astrology are attributed</note>. For **HERMES** wills that one should hide these gifts of **GOD** from all unwise men and fools. **MACROBIUS** <note>A 5th-century Roman provincial writer known for his commentary on Cicero, often cited regarding the use of allegory to protect philosophical truths</note> also writes that one should obscure and describe great secret things with hidden words and speeches. Thus **THEOPHRASTUS** <note>Paracelsus</note> used words that are known neither to you nor to me, and even if one does not understand them, one should not immediately denounce them as lies and fables. But so that I do not make this writing long, I will briefly report how many things there are from which each thing is born and made.

He argues that Paracelsus's difficult terminology is a traditional way to protect divine knowledge from the unworthy.</summary>

**THEOPHRASTUS** <note>Theophrastus von Hohenheim, known as Paracelsus (1493–1541), the Swiss-German physician and chemist who revolutionized medicine</note> writes in the *Paragranum* <note>original: "Paragrano"; one of Paracelsus's fundamental texts outlining the four pillars of medicine: Philosophy, Astronomy, Alchemy, and Virtue</note> how it is evident and clearer than the bright sunshine that all **metals** <note>original: "Metalla"</note> do not grow from two things alone—namely **Sulfur** and **Mercury**—but rather from three. It is this third element <note>Paracelsus introduced "Salt" as the third principle, forming the *Tria Prima* or Three Primes</note> that coagulates the other two and brings them into one **body** <note>original Latin: "Corpus"</note>. He says that because of the focus on Mercury and Sulfur alone, the philosophers were deceived, fell into error, and it was as if their very legs had been pulled out and taken from them. Through this ignorance, many have been led astray; and after they have frequently miscarried <note>original: "fehl gebohren"; a metaphor for failed alchemical experiments</note> their attempts, they have brought **alchemy** into contempt, so that it has gained an evil reputation as if it were a deceiver. I can understand and conclude this much from the writings of Theophrastus: that he knew the **Philosopher’s Stone** <note>original: "Stein der Weisen"</note> and used it in **medicine**, and that it is not a poem or a work of fables, as the common man believes it to be.

This has moved me, and for that reason I can well tolerate this letter of mine coming into public print, so that not everyone who is inexperienced in these matters should undertake them in an ignorant fashion. Otherwise, they might seek this most hidden **secret** <note>original Latin: "Secretum"</note> and **Golden Fleece** <note>original Latin: "aurem Vellus"; a mythological reference to the ultimate prize, often used by alchemists to represent the goal of the Great Work</note> with the loss of their money and time, and learn of it only through their own injury. Therefore, let a person be reminded beforehand and look to what he intends to do and undertake. I have dissolved <note>original: "solvirt"</note> and unlocked **lead** <note>original: "Bley"</note>, in which I found an **oil**, a **mercury**, and an **earth**; whether now such...

</margin>
